issues.title: Add ix mcp subcommand: expose ix as a local MCP server
issues.body:
## Summary

Add an `ix mcp` subcommand that runs ix as a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Exposes a curated set of read + write tools to MCP-aware AI clients (Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, etc.) so the model can invoke ix operations directly without going through shell subprocess invocations.

This is **orthogonal to and complementary with `--format llm` (#206)**, not a replacement. `--format llm` shrinks the output payload; MCP changes how the call is made and discovered. Tool handlers internally render with the same compact format defined in #206.

## Motivation

Today, AI agents invoke ix via shell:
- ix-claude-plugin hooks shell out to `ix text`, `ix overview`, etc. and inject results as `additionalContext`.
- Skills under `skills/` instruct the model to run `ix <cmd> --format json` in its reasoning, which Claude Code executes as a `Bash` tool call.

This is fine but has friction:
- **Model has to know about ix.** The CLAUDE.md routing table is ~3-4 KB of context loaded into every session teaching the model what commands exist.
- **Shell escaping is fragile.** See #196 — multi-line patterns and backslash escapes blew up because the hook concatenated shell strings. MCP passes args as structured JSON; this class of bug disappears.
- **Per-invocation overhead.** Each shell call spawns a Node process (~50-200 ms before any actual work). For fast commands (`ix locate`, `ix entity`) startup dominates. A long-lived MCP server amortizes this.
- **No tool discovery.** Adding a new command requires updating CLAUDE.md prose. With MCP, tool schemas are auto-discovered at session start.

MCP solves the *transport + discovery* problem. `--format llm` solves the *payload size* problem. Both stack: a session that uses both gets the byte savings of `--format llm` on tool responses plus the discovery and shell-escape wins of MCP.

## Where the code lives

`ix mcp` subcommand inside `ix-cli`. Considered alternatives:

| | Approach | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| ix-cli subcommand (this proposal) | New `ix mcp` in this repo | OK. Single source of truth, reuses existing handlers + renderers, no version skew, works for every MCP client |
| Plugin-side wrapper in ix-claude-plugin | Plugin ships an MCP server that shells out to `ix` per call | Rejected. Reimplements logic, doesn't help other AI tools, per-call subprocess cost |
| Standalone `ix-mcp` repo | New repo, depends on the @ix/client package | Rejected. Three-repo coordination burden, separate release cadence |

Files (new):
- `ix-cli/src/cli/commands/mcp.ts` — registers `ix mcp` subcommand
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/server.ts` — MCP server boilerplate (uses `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`)
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/tools/index.ts` — tool registry
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/tools/<command>.ts` — one file per tool, exposes the tool's JSON schema and wraps the existing CLI handler
- `ix-cli/src/mcp/format.ts` — shared response formatter, delegates to the `--format llm` renderers
- `docs/mcp.md` — user-facing setup guide

## Transport

**stdio only in v1.** Client spawns `ix mcp` as a subprocess; JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout. SSE/HTTP transports add lifecycle and security surface we don't need. If a remote use case appears, that is a v3 addition with explicit auth design.

## Tool catalog (v1 — 28 tools)

Tools map roughly 1:1 to CLI commands the model already invokes per CLAUDE.md routing. Naming is flat (`search`, `locate`, etc.); MCP clients namespace by server name (e.g., `ix:search` in Claude Code).

### Read tools — navigate (10)
`search`, `locate`, `explain`, `read`, `entity`, `overview`, `inventory`, `rank`, `stats`, `text`

### Read tools — relationships (6)
`callers`, `callees`, `contains`, `imports`, `imported_by`, `depends`

### Read tools — structural analysis (3)
`smells`, `subsystems`, `impact`

### Read tools — history & decisions (4)
`history`, `decisions`, `conflicts`, `briefing`

### Write tools (5, Pro-gated)
`decide`, `bug_create`, `bug_update`, `goal_create`, `plan_create`

Write tools are annotated as destructive in their MCP descriptions so clients (Claude Code, Cursor) can apply per-call confirmation policies.

### Deliberately not in v1
- `map`, `ingest` — expensive (seconds to minutes); defer to v2 with explicit time-cost annotations
- `docker`, `instance`, `status`, `doctor`, `upgrade`, `view`, `reset`, `config`, `savings` — ops/admin, not model-invoked
- `query` — deprecated per CLAUDE.md
- `diff`, `patches` — niche; add when explicit demand appears
- Workflow-aggregated tools (`investigate`, `audit`, `discover`) — see v2 below

## User controls (toggling tools and the server)

Users should be able to constrain what the MCP server exposes without editing every plugin manifest that registers it. v1 ships four layers of control, each addressing a different threat model:

### 1. Server kill switch
- Env: `IX_MCP_ENABLED=false`
- Config: `mcp.enabled: false` in `~/.ix/config`
- When disabled, `ix mcp` exits immediately with a clear stderr message. The MCP client treats this as server-not-available and falls back to whatever the model would do without ix tools.
- Use case: user doesn't want MCP at all, even if a plugin registers it.

### 2. Read-only mode
- Flag: `ix mcp --read-only`
- Env: `IX_MCP_READ_ONLY=1`
- Disables all 5 write tools (`decide`, `bug_create`, `bug_update`, `goal_create`, `plan_create`). Server still advertises the 23 read tools.
- Use case: CI runs, sandboxed contexts, demos, untrusted-model paths, "I want navigation but no state mutations."

### 3. Per-tool allowlist / blocklist
- `ix mcp --enable-tools search,locate,overview` — explicit allowlist (most restrictive)
- `ix mcp --disable-tools decide,read` — blocklist (more common)
- Env equivalents: `IX_MCP_ENABLED_TOOLS`, `IX_MCP_DISABLED_TOOLS`
- Same values readable from `~/.ix/config` so users don't repeat them per session
- Allowlist wins if both are set (warn at startup).
- Use case: lock down to a known-good subset; reduce session-context cost from tool descriptions.

### 4. Per-call confirmation (client-side)
Write tools are annotated as `destructive` in MCP tool metadata. Compatible clients (Claude Code, Cursor) honor the annotation and prompt the user before each call. The server just emits the annotation; the actual prompt policy lives with the client.
- Use case: "I'm OK with this tool existing but want explicit consent each time."

### Defaults
All four default to permissive: server enabled, full toolset, no filter, destructive annotation present (so client-side confirmation kicks in for writes). Users opt into restriction.

## Tool response format

Each tool returns `--format llm`-style text by default, optionally JSON if the caller passes `format: "json"` in its args. Internally, tool handlers call the same renderers Ix#206 ships. The MCP layer adds no per-call rendering; it just selects which renderer to invoke.

This is why **Ix#206 (`--format llm`) must land first**. The MCP server's reason for existing token-wise is to deliver compact responses; if `--format llm` isn't ready, the MCP server has nothing to render with.

## Config and auth

Reuse the existing CLI mechanisms with no new surface:
- Env: `IX_ENDPOINT`, `IX_ORG_ID`, `IX_HOME`, `IX_DEBUG`
- Files: `~/.ix/config`, workspace `.ix/config`
- The MCP server is the same logical client as `ix` CLI; same `IxClient`, same `getEndpoint`.

The server probes backend health and schema version at startup (same as today's CLI commands).

## State and caching

V1: stateless. Each tool call hits the backend. No in-process cache.

V2 follow-up: TTL cache for read-heavy reads (`entity`, `overview`, `read`) that don't change mid-session. Per-tool TTLs.

## Build / install impact

- New dependency: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` (~50 KB minified, no native bindings)
- Bundle size of `ix` increases marginally; no install-script changes
- `ix mcp` is discoverable via `ix --help` so users find it the same way they find other subcommands

## Test strategy

- **Unit:** per-tool handler tests with mocked `IxClient`, assert schema validation and response shape
- **Integration:** spin up `ix mcp` as a subprocess in a vitest test, drive it with the MCP client SDK, assert tool list + call responses against running memory-layer
- **Manual:** Claude Code and Cursor sessions with the server registered; verify auto-discovery, tool execution, error paths

## Adopter-side work

Tracked in ix-infrastructure/ix-claude-plugin#22 (analogous to plugin#21 for `--format llm`). Scope on the plugin side:
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` gets an `mcpServers.ix` entry pointing at `ix mcp`
- Skills under `skills/` migrate from `ix <cmd> --format json` invocations to `ix:<tool>` MCP tool calls where the call is model-invoked
- Hooks under `hooks/` stay on CLI; they fire on shell events, not model events, so MCP doesn't help them

Other adopters (ix-cursor-plugin, ix-codex-plugin, ix-opencode-plugin, ix-gemini-plugin) get analogous adoption issues filed in their respective repos.

## Decisions locked in

- **Subcommand name:** `ix mcp`
- **Transport:** stdio only in v1
- **Code home:** ix-cli subcommand (Option A from the alternatives table)
- **Tool naming:** flat names (`search`, `subsystems`, ...); MCP clients namespace by server
- **Response format:** delegates to `--format llm` renderers from Ix#206; not a separate format
- **Config:** reuses existing `IxClient`/env/config files, no new mechanism
- **State:** stateless v1; caching deferred to v2
- **User controls:** four-layer model (server kill switch, read-only mode, per-tool allow/blocklist, MCP-annotated destructive flag for client-side confirmation). All default to permissive.
- **Per-call confirmation:** server emits the `destructive` annotation on write tools; the actual per-call prompt policy lives with the MCP client.

## Out of scope for v1 (named explicitly so they don't sneak in)

- Workflow-aggregated tools (`investigate`, `audit`, etc.); design once we have v1 usage data
- Streaming responses
- Result caching
- `map`, `ingest`, or any expensive/destructive operation
- SSE / remote transport
- Server-side rate limiting or per-session metrics
- Auth beyond the existing IxClient mechanism

## Open questions

1. **Write tools in v1?** Currently planned to ship 5 write tools (`decide`, `bug_create`, etc.) annotated as destructive so clients can prompt; the new `--read-only` flag lets users disable them per-session. Alternative: defer all write tools to v2 and keep v1 purely read-only. Trade-off: read-only v1 ships sooner with smaller surface; write-included v1 means skills don't need to fall back to CLI for the write paths.
2. **Tool description length budget.** Every tool description is permanent session context. Cap at ~150 chars/tool? At 28 tools that is a 4 KB ceiling.
3. **Subcommand visibility:** should `ix mcp` show up in `ix --help`? Lean yes; discoverability beats hiding.

## Dependencies and sequencing

Hard prerequisite: **Ix#206 (`--format llm`) must land first**, at least Tier 1 renderers. MCP tool responses depend on having compact renderers to call into. Once `--format llm` PR 1 ships, MCP work can begin.

## v2 / v3 follow-ups (not this issue)

- v2: workflow-aggregated tools, result caching, streaming for large responses, `map`/`ingest` exposure
- v3: SSE/HTTP transport for remote scenarios, MCP "resources" exposure (graph nodes as resources), subscribe-style updates

issues.title: [bug] Windows installer — path with spaces
issues.body:
## Description

The Windows installer fails during CLI installation when the Windows user profile/TEMP path contains a space.

In my case, the user profile is `C:\Users\Win 10`. The CLI archive downloads and extracts successfully, but the installer then resolves part of the path as `C:\Users\WIN10\~1` and fails because that path does not exist.

Using a TEMP directory without spaces allows the installation to complete successfully.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a Windows account with a profile path containing a space, such as `C:\Users\Win 10`.
2. Run:

   ```powershell
   irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex
   ```
3. Wait for the CLI installation stage after the archive has been downloaded and extracted.

## Expected behavior

The installer should correctly handle Windows user profile and temporary paths containing spaces and complete the CLI installation.

## Actual behavior

The archive downloads and extracts successfully, but the installer fails while resolving the temporary path.

Changing `TEMP` and `TMP` to a path without spaces, such as `C:\Temp`, allows the installation to succeed.

## CLI output

```text
[ok] Downloaded to C:\Users\WIN10\~1\AppData\Local\Temp\ix-0.8.1-windows-amd64.zip
Extracting CLI...
[ok] Extraction complete

Ix installer failed.
Error:
An object at the specified path C:\Users\WIN10\~1 does not exist.
```

## Environment

* OS: Windows
* Node: v24.18.0
* Ix version: 0.8.1

comments.body:
Reopening: closed automatically by the #352 merge, but the fix is not yet confirmed to resolve this.

#352 **has** shipped and is worth trying — it routes the installer's two scratch files (the CLI zip and the compose pull log) out of `TEMP` and into `IX_HOME`, which comes from `USERPROFILE` in its long form. Since you confirmed that pointing `TEMP`/`TMP` at a path without a space lets the install finish, moving off `TEMP` should fix it. `install.ps1` is served from `main`, so it is live now — no release needed.

But the mechanism the PR described did not hold up, and nobody has reproduced this on a machine with the failing profile, so the issue should stay open until you can confirm. Specifically:

- PowerShell's FileSystem provider **does** resolve 8.3 short segments on both Windows PowerShell 5.1 and 7 — `Test-Path C:\PROGRA~1` returns `True`, and `Get-Item`, `Expand-Archive` and `Remove-Item` all work on a real `WIN10~1` path.
- Your transcript shows the installer reaching `[ok] Extraction complete`. The two provider calls on the zip (`Test-Path -LiteralPath`, `Get-Item -LiteralPath`) run *before* extraction, so they succeeded on that short path.
- `An object at the specified path ... does not exist.` could not be reproduced from any of ~30 path-taking cmdlets, including every one the installer calls on those paths — they report `Cannot find path` instead.

The most likely remaining explanation is that 8.3 alias *creation* is disabled on that volume while `TEMP` still holds a stale short path, so nothing resolves it. #352 fixes that reading too, which is why it shipped.

**If you are able to help confirm**, two things would settle it:

1. Re-run `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex` on the affected account with `TEMP`/`TMP` back at their original values, and say whether it completes.
2. If it still fails, the full error would pin it:
   ```powershell
   $env:TEMP
   fsutil 8dot3name query C:
   Test-Path $env:TEMP
   $Error[0] | Format-List * -Force
   ```

One small thing worth checking either way: the output above quotes the path as `C:\Users\WIN10\~1`, with a backslash before `~1`. We assumed that is a copy/paste artifact and the real path is `C:\Users\WIN10~1` (the 8.3 alias of `C:\Users\Win 10`), since a literal `~1` directory would be unusual — but if your console really did print it with the backslash, that changes the diagnosis and is worth knowing.

Thanks for the detailed report — the `TEMP`-without-spaces datapoint is what made the fix actionable.

Thank you for the issue — the detail that a space-free TEMP directory worked was the clue that made this diagnosable, and `C:\Users\Win 10` → `C:\Users\WIN10~1` is the whole bug in one line.

The fix is **merged** in #352: the installer was mixing 8.3 short paths with long-path APIs, so it resolved a path it was never asked to write.

**Deliberately keeping this open** rather than auto-closing it. #352 was filed with `Refs #349` instead of `Fixes #349` precisely so merging would not close this before someone confirms it on a real Windows profile with a space in the path — the fix was verified by other means, not on the machine that hit it.

If you get the chance to re-run the installer on that account after the next release, a confirmation here would be very welcome and I will close it out. No obligation — I will get it verified either way.

The fix shipped in #352 and is on `main`: the installer's scratch files (`.cli-staging-<pid>.zip` and its pull log) now live under `$IX_HOME`, which comes from `USERPROFILE` in long form, instead of under `TEMP` — taking the script off the 8.3-shortened path the failure was traced to.

Deliberately merged as `Refs #349` rather than `Fixes`, so this stayed open pending a real run. Worth restating what is *not* established, because it affects how the verification should be read: the mechanism was never reproduced. The provider cmdlets this script calls resolve 8.3 segments fine on both 5.1 and 7, and no cmdlet the installer invokes produces the reported error string. The likeliest remaining explanation is that 8.3 alias creation is disabled on that volume while `TEMP` still carries a stale short path — moving off `TEMP` fixes that reading too, which is why it was worth shipping ahead of the diagnosis.

@RMA1313 — if you still have that machine, a plain `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex` with `TEMP`/`TMP` left at their defaults would settle it.

One thing this did **not** cover: `ix upgrade` still stages through `os.tmpdir()`, which on Windows is `TEMP` verbatim. If this class of failure is real, it is unfixed there — and would show up as a broken upgrade rather than a broken install.

Verified end to end on a real Windows machine on 2026-08-13. Closing as fixed.

Environment:
- Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200 (build 26200)
- Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100.9168
- Node v26.7.0
- live `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex`
- installer selected Ix v0.9.3

I ran two fresh, isolated installs:

1. `USERPROFILE=C:\Users\josep\Ix 349 Test`, with `TEMP`/`TMP=C:\Users\josep\Ix 349 Test\AppData\Local\Temp`.
2. `USERPROFILE=C:\Users\josep\Ix 349 Stale`, with `TEMP`/`TMP=C:\Users\IX349T~1\AppData\Local\Temp`; that short-style path deliberately did not exist (`Test-Path` was false before and after the run), matching the likeliest stale-8.3-path explanation discussed above.

Both runs completed the real CLI path successfully:

- the archive downloaded under the long-form profile path in `$IX_HOME`, not under `TEMP`
- extraction completed
- the CLI installed
- the generated launcher independently returned `0.9.3`
- no `.cli-staging-*` artifacts remained

Docker Compose was stubbed for test isolation so this did not touch the machine's real containers; the live installer download, release ZIP download, PowerShell extraction, directory swap, launcher creation, and CLI execution were all real. The original failure is in that tested CLI path.

This confirms #352 fixes the installer even when `TEMP` is unusable, not merely when it contains a space. #392 also moved `ix upgrade` downloads off `TEMP`, covering the related upgrade path.

issues.title: ix patches is registered nowhere — registerPatchesCommand is dead code
issues.body:
Found by @Alot1z while writing the agent skill (#368).

\`ix-cli/src/cli/commands/patches.ts:6\` exports \`registerPatchesCommand\`, but nothing imports it — it is absent from \`ix-cli/src/cli/register/oss.ts\`. So \`ix patches\` is an unknown command today.

It is also listed in \`PRO_COMMANDS\` in \`oss.ts\`, which means \`registerProStubs\` currently installs the "requires Ix Pro" stub for it. Users on Pro presumably get the real one; users on OSS get the Pro message rather than an unknown-command error, which is why this has gone unnoticed.

Decide which it is:
- If \`patches\` is meant to be OSS, register it in \`oss.ts\` and drop it from \`PRO_COMMANDS\`.
- If it is meant to be Pro-only, delete \`patches.ts\` from this repo so the stub is the only implementation.

Note the file already carries a complete \`--format <fmt>\` declaration advertising \`llm\`, with no llm renderer behind it — see the \`--format llm\` coverage issue.

issues.title: [bug] JS and TS calls disappear across 500-file parse batches
issues.body:
## Description

`ix map` resolves JavaScript and TypeScript calls differently depending on which 500-file parse batch contains the caller and callee. A caller parsed before its imported definition loses its `CALLS` edge, while an equivalent caller in the definition's batch resolves correctly.

This makes `ix callers`, `ix callees`, and `ix impact` undercount production usage and can produce a low-risk assessment for a widely used symbol.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create a fresh TypeScript repository with 515 tracked files.
2. Put `src/a-consumer.ts` near the start of `git ls-files`:

```ts
import { crossBatchTarget } from "src/z-target";

export function runCrossBatchTarget(): number {
  return crossBatchTarget();
}
```

3. Add 510 filler TypeScript files so that `src/z-target.ts` is outside the first 500-file batch:

```ts
export function crossBatchTarget(): number {
  return 42;
}
```

4. Add `src/zz-consumer.ts` after the target with the same import and call pattern.
5. Configure `baseUrl` as `.`, then run:

```sh
ix map . --silent
ix impact crossBatchTarget --kind function --depth 2 --format json
ix callees runCrossBatchTarget --kind function --format json
```

## Expected behavior

Both `runCrossBatchTarget` and the same-batch consumer are callers of `crossBatchTarget`. The early consumer's `callees` result contains `crossBatchTarget`.

## Actual behavior

Only the consumer in the target's batch is reported. The earlier consumer has no resolved callee.

The path-only global index identifies `src/z-target.ts`, but JavaScript and TypeScript definitions are not included in `fileQKeys` or `fileHasSymbol`. `resolveEdges` therefore cannot verify the imported destination and drops the cross-batch `CALLS` edge.

## CLI output

```json
{
  "summary": {
    "callers": 1,
    "callees": 0
  },
  "callerList": [
    {
      "kind": "function",
      "name": "runSameBatchTarget"
    }
  ]
}
```

`ix callees runCrossBatchTarget` returns zero results.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: 0.9.1

comments.body:
Thank you for the issue — and for fixing it in the same breath. The report is precise about the mechanism (definitions landing in a later streamed batch than the caller), which is what made #375 straightforward to review against.

Tracked by **#375**, which is open with review comments. It carries `Fixes #374`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The change itself is correct — the index construction mirrors `resolveEdges`' in-batch path exactly, so cross-batch and in-batch resolution agree on `dstQualifiedKey`. My open question is cost, not correctness: the prescan parses synchronously on the main thread while the streaming loop uses a worker pool, so every unchanged JS/TS file is re-read and re-parsed on each incremental `ix map`. Details and measurements are on the PR.

issues.title: ix upgrade compares two unrelated version series to decide if Compass is stale
issues.body:
The bundled Compass is stamped with the **Ix** version; `ix-compass-dist` releases use their **own** series. `isNewer` compares them directly, so the check is only accidentally correct.

Verified on the shipped v0.9.1 linux tarball:

```
compass/.version = 0.9.1          # the Ix version, not a compass version
```

and the latest `ix-compass-dist` release is **v0.3.0** (2026-08-09).

`upgrade.ts` does `isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` — `isNewer("0.3.0", "0.9.1")` → `false`, so nothing happens and `ix view` keeps the correct bundled build. That is the right outcome, but only because Ix's numbers currently happen to be larger.

**The moment `ix-compass-dist` tags anything above the running Ix version** — v1.0.0, or just v0.9.2 — `isNewer` returns true and `ix upgrade` replaces a correct, newer bundled Compass with the dist build. That is the same failure v0.9.1 just fixed (#365/#366), reached by a different route: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

Options:
- Stamp the bundle with the **compass** version the release was built from (v0.3.0 was built from `system-compass@7f98724`), so both sides of the comparison are the same series.
- Or stamp the source commit and compare identity rather than order — the question is really "is the installed bundle the one this CLI shipped with", not "is it numerically older".

Either way, `getInstalledCompassVersion` and `writeCache(compassLatest)` should not be feeding two different numbering schemes into one `isNewer`.

issues.title: [bug] Remapping keeps deleted and renamed symbols in the graph
issues.body:
## Description

After a successful incremental `ix map`, symbols removed by a rename or file deletion remain queryable in the graph. A deleted file can report a clean workspace even though its old nodes and incident edges are still present.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create a small TypeScript project with `src/provider.ts` exporting `removedTarget` and `src/caller.ts` importing and calling it.
2. Run `ix map . --silent` and confirm `ix callers removedTarget --format json` returns the caller.
3. Either rename `removedTarget` in both files or delete `src/provider.ts`.
4. Run `ix map . --silent` again.
5. Run `ix locate removedTarget --format json`.

## Expected behavior

Entities no longer emitted by the current source should be removed with their incident edges. If a deleted provider file is later recreated, surviving callers should be re-ingested so their dependency edges are restored.

## Actual behavior

The old symbol remains resolvable after a rename, so repeated renames accumulate stale graph entities. Deleting the provider also leaves its old symbol and caller edge behind even though the map finishes successfully.

## CLI output

After deleting the provider and remapping with Ix 0.9.1:

```text
$ ix map . --silent
map: 3 files ...

$ ix locate removedTarget --format json
"resolvedTarget": { "kind": "function", "name": "removedTarget", "path": "src/provider.ts" }
```

## Environment
- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: 26.7.0
- Ix version: 0.9.1

comments.body:
Thank you for the issue — this is a real gap, and one that quietly corrupts the graph rather than failing loudly, which makes it worth more than its size suggests.

Tracked by **#378**, which is open with review comments and currently conflicting with `main`. It carries `Fixes #377`, so this will close automatically when that lands.

The approach is right (compare the previous patch manifest, emit explicit deletions, track dependents so a recreated file heals its callers). The blocking item on the PR is that `reconcileRemovedEntities` runs before `stripMapModeOps`, which means `ix map` after `ix ingest` deletes chunk nodes it never recreates — reproduced on the branch. Detail on the PR.

issues.title: [bug] --kind silently selects among duplicate same-kind symbols
issues.body:
## Description

Passing `--kind` can silently select the first result when multiple exact-name candidates have the same requested kind. Because resolution completes before ambiguity handling, an accompanying `--pick` is ignored as well.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create two TypeScript files that each export a class named `DuplicateService`.
2. Give the first class one member and the second class two members so the selected target is observable.
3. Run `ix map . --silent`.
4. Run `ix impact DuplicateService --kind class --format json`.
5. Run `ix impact DuplicateService --kind class --pick 2 --format json`.

## Expected behavior

`--kind class` should filter out other kinds but remain ambiguous when multiple classes still match. Adding `--pick 2` should select the second class.

## Actual behavior

Both commands silently select the first class and report one member. The second command ignores `--pick 2`.

Without `--kind`, the same fixture correctly reports both candidates:

```text
Ambiguous symbol "DuplicateService":
  1. class ... DuplicateService in src/alpha/DuplicateService.ts
  2. class ... DuplicateService in src/beta/DuplicateService.ts
```

## CLI output

```json
{
  "resolvedTarget": {
    "kind": "class",
    "name": "DuplicateService"
  },
  "summary": {
    "members": 1
  }
}
```

The output remains the same with `--kind class --pick 2`, although the second class has two members.

## Environment
- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: 26.7.0
- Ix version: 0.9.1 and current `main`

comments.body:
Thank you for the issue. You framed the underlying principle exactly right: `--kind` is a *filter*, not a *tiebreaker*, and silently analysing the wrong symbol is worse than asking which one was meant.

Tracked by **#380**, which is approved and carries `Fixes #379`, so this will close automatically when it lands.

issues.title: [bug] Codex hooks and CLI subprocess calls fail on native Windows
issues.body:
## Description

The official Ix Codex integration installs on native Windows, and the Ix CLI/backend work, but the installed Codex hooks cannot execute. This prevents automatic context injection and graph refresh unless users patch the installed integration locally.

There appear to be two independent Windows process-launching problems:

1. The generated Codex hook commands use `/bin/sh -lc ...`. Native Windows does not provide `/bin/sh`.
2. The installed Python integration invokes `ix` with calls such as `subprocess.run(["ix", ...])` / `Popen(["ix", ...])`. On Windows, the installed command is `ix.cmd`. Python's Windows `CreateProcess` cannot execute a `.cmd` file directly without a command shell, so these calls fail with `WinError 2`, even though `shutil.which("ix")` resolves `ix.CMD` and the same command works interactively in PowerShell.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install Ix on Windows using the official PowerShell installer.
2. Install the official Codex integration/plugin.
3. Confirm that Ix itself works:

   ```powershell
   ix status --format json
   ```

4. Start Codex with hooks enabled and perform an action that should trigger an Ix hook.
5. Alternatively, run a minimal Python probe:

   ```python
   import shutil
   import subprocess

   print(shutil.which("ix"))  # resolves ...\ix.CMD
   subprocess.run(["ix", "status", "--format", "json"], check=True)
   ```

## Expected behavior

The official Codex integration should work on native Windows without modifying installed Ix/plugin files:

- hook commands should use a platform-compatible launcher;
- Python subprocess calls should launch the Windows CLI correctly;
- automatic Ix context injection and graph refresh should operate after installation.

## Actual behavior

- hook commands referencing `/bin/sh` cannot start on native Windows;
- direct Python subprocess calls to `ix` fail with `FileNotFoundError: [WinError 2]`;
- the CLI itself works normally when invoked from PowerShell as `ix`.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 Home, 10.0.26200
- PowerShell: 7.6.3
- Node.js: 22.23.0
- Python: 3.14.4
- Codex CLI: 0.147.0
- Ix: 0.9.1
- Ix Codex plugin: 2.4.0

## Request

Please make the generated Codex integration platform-aware so native Windows users can use the official hooks without local patches. Keeping generated/installed plugin files unmodified is important because local edits are overwritten or may conflict with future Ix updates.

comments.body:
Both causes are now covered, in the plugin repo — mirrored there as ix-codex-plugin#22, because GitHub closing keywords do not work across repositories and this issue would otherwise never auto-close.

| cause | fix |
|---|---|
| `/bin/sh -lc` in all five `hooks.json` commands | ix-codex-plugin#20 |
| `subprocess` not consulting `PATHEXT` for `ix.CMD` | ix-codex-plugin#19 |

Worth being explicit that **neither alone is enough**: #19's fix lives inside `common.py`, and until #20 lands the hook process never starts, so that code never runs. #19's own description scopes it to "the half that breaks the CLI" — it is the half that is unreachable without the other.

Leaving this open. Neither PR has been run on real Windows; both were written and tested on Linux, where the changed paths are no-ops or unit-tested in isolation. @tept-creator — a confirmation from a real Windows box after both merge is what should close this.

Verified end to end on native Windows on 2026-08-13. Closing as fixed.

Environment:
- Windows 11 Home, build 26200
- PowerShell 7.6.4
- Python 3.14.7
- Ix 0.9.3 (`C:\Users\josep\AppData\Roaming\npm\ix.CMD`)
- ix-codex-plugin 2.4.1 at current `main` commit `6bcdeb1689b23e60bd1059e494a4b032e6f87889`

Verification:

1. Ran the focused Windows suites on Windows itself: 40 tests passed (`test_ix_argv_resolution` and `test_windows_hook_launch`; one POSIX-only case skipped).
2. Installed the official integration with `install.ps1 --repo <spaced path> --hooks --mode copy --force` into `...\Issue 383 Target`.
3. Confirmed the installed `hooks.json` rewrote all five `/bin/sh` commands to the absolute native Python executable plus `_launch.py`; both paths were correctly quoted and there were no `/bin/sh` references left.
4. Executed every installed command through native `cmd.exe`, from a nested working directory so `_launch.py` had to locate the project hooks:
   - SessionStart: exit 0
   - UserPromptSubmit: exit 0
   - PreToolUse: exit 0
   - PostToolUse: exit 0
   - Stop: exit 0 (`{"continue": true}`)
5. Imported the installed `common.py` and called its real `run_command(["ix", "--version"])`. It resolved the bare command to `C:\Users\josep\AppData\Roaming\npm\ix.CMD`, launched it successfully, and returned `0.9.3` with exit 0.

That exercises both required halves on native Windows: #20's shell-free launcher and #19's PATHEXT-aware `.CMD` subprocess resolution, including the background-map launcher path reached by Stop. The original hook launch failure and `WinError 2` are resolved.

issues.title: [bug] ix upgrade breaks Windows CLI when upgrading from 0.8.1 to 0.9.1
issues.body:
## Description

Running `ix upgrade` on Windows broke the installed Ix CLI while upgrading from version `0.8.1` to `0.9.1`.

Before the upgrade, `ix` worked normally. After the upgrade completed, invoking `ix` failed because the generated wrapper at `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd` pointed to a CLI path that no longer existed.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start with a working Ix `0.8.1` installation on Windows.
2. Run:

   ```powershell
   ix upgrade
   ```
3. After upgrading to `0.9.1`, run:

   ```powershell
   ix
   ```

## Expected behavior

`ix upgrade` should upgrade the CLI in place and leave the `ix` command functional.

After upgrading, `ix --version` should report `0.9.1` and all existing commands should continue to work.

## Actual behavior

After upgrading from `0.8.1` to `0.9.1`, the `ix` command became unusable.

The wrapper under:

```text
C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\ix.cmd
```

attempted to execute:

```text
C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd
```

but that target was no longer available after the upgrade.

Re-running the full Windows installer restored the CLI.

## CLI output

```text
PS C:\Users\Win 10\Documents\project\coin> ix

'"C:\Users\Win 10\.ix\bin\..\cli\ix.cmd"' is not recognized as an internal or external command,
operable program or batch file.
```

## Environment

* OS: Windows
* Node: v24.18.0
* Ix version before upgrade: 0.8.1
* Ix version being upgraded to: 0.9.1

comments.body:
Thank you for the issue — this is an unusually good report. Naming the exact path the wrapper tried to execute is what made it diagnosable in one pass, and noting that reinstalling restored it confirmed the cause before anyone had to reproduce it.

## Unblocking you now

```powershell
irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

That rewrites the launcher and restores the CLI, which matches what you already found. You should not need to uninstall first, and your graph and config are untouched — the breakage is only in `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`.

## What happened

You were on the wrong side of a one-way door.

`ix upgrade` before 0.9.0 refreshed only the **bash** shim (the one Git Bash uses) and never touched `~\.ix\bin\ix.cmd`, which is the launcher native PowerShell actually runs. Meanwhile the upgrade extracted the new CLI into a **version-nested** directory, so `~\.ix\cli\ix.cmd` — the path your launcher points at — stopped existing. Your wrapper was left aimed at a file the upgrade had just moved.

The layout half of this was fixed in #346 and shipped in v0.9.0. The catch is that `ix upgrade` is run by the version you are upgrading *from*, so 0.8.1 executed 0.8.1's code and the fix could not participate. **Anyone going from ≤0.8.1 to 0.9.x on Windows hits this**, and no change we ship can prevent it retroactively — which is precisely why it deserved its own fix rather than a "already fixed, please upgrade" reply.

Once you are on 0.9.1, future upgrades go through `refreshLaunchers()`, which rewrites the launcher for either layout. This is a one-time cost.

## What is changing

#386 makes the launcher diagnose itself. It checks its target before invoking it and, when it is missing, prints the cause and the reinstall command instead of cmd.exe's message naming the wrapper. That has to live in the batch file: at that point `ix doctor` is exactly as unreachable as `ix`, so nothing inside the CLI can reach you.

Your report also turned up a second bug in the same three lines: the old launcher never propagated the exit code, so **every** non-zero `ix` exit was reported to callers as success. That has been fixed alongside it.

I am leaving this issue open until someone confirms the new launcher on real Windows — I do not have a machine to run cmd.exe on, and I would rather not close it on tests alone.

One question, if you have a moment: does `ix --version` report `0.9.1` after reinstalling? That tells us whether the upgrade had already staged the new CLI correctly and only the launcher was wrong, or whether the payload needed replacing too.

Status check, since three separate changes touch this and it is not obvious from the outside which of them closes it.

**The forward path is complete.** Traced end to end on `main`:

- the release archive carries `ix.cmd` at its top level (`release.yml:309`), so the file the shim targets is genuinely in the tarball;
- `install.ps1` collapses that top level into a flat `$IX_HOME\cli\`, which is why `%~dp0..\cli\ix.cmd` resolves (#346, v0.9.0);
- `ix upgrade` re-derives the same layout — `soleChildDir(installDir) ?? installDir` (`upgrade.ts:1026`) — and `refreshLaunchers()` rewrites `bin\ix.cmd` to match, flat or nested, on every upgrade.

So an upgrade **from v0.9.0 or later** rewrites the shim to a target that exists.

**What cannot be fixed forward** is the population this was reported from: `ix upgrade` is executed by the version being upgraded *from*, so nothing shipped today reaches a v0.8.1 install. #386 is the recovery for exactly that — the launcher now checks its target before invoking it and prints the reinstall command, because once broken, `ix doctor` is as unreachable as `ix`.

**What is still missing is a Windows run.** Every piece above is asserted by tests and has never been executed by `cmd.exe` — #386 shipped as `Refs`, not `Fixes`, for that reason. This wants:

1. a v0.9.1 → v0.9.2 upgrade, confirming `ix --version` still works afterwards, and
2. a deliberately broken `bin\ix.cmd` (point it at a nonexistent target), confirming the recovery message prints rather than the raw `is not recognized` error.

That is what should close this, not another patch. Same standing requirement as #349 and #383.

Verified on native Windows on 2026-08-13. Closing as fixed.

Environment:
- Windows 11 Home, build 26200
- Windows PowerShell 5.1 for installation; PowerShell 7.6.4 for upgrade/launcher checks
- Node v26.7.0

Forward-upgrade check:

1. Used the live installer with `IX_VERSION=0.9.1` to create a fresh, working install under the spaced profile path `C:\Users\josep\Ix 385 Test`.
2. Restricted PATH to that isolated `bin\ix.cmd`, Node, Windows tools, and a Docker stub. `where ix` returned only the isolated launcher; the real npm launcher was SHA-256 checked before and after and stayed byte-identical.
3. Invoked the real v0.9.1 CLI's own `ix upgrade`. It selected current v0.9.3 and completed with exit 0:
   - `Upgraded ix: 0.9.1 → 0.9.3`
   - `ix --version` afterwards returned `0.9.3` with exit 0
   - `$IX_HOME\cli\ix.cmd` existed

This is the requested v0.9.1→newer forward-path check, using v0.9.3 rather than v0.9.2 because that is now the current release.

Broken-launcher recovery check:

1. Re-ran the live v0.9.3 installer so `bin\ix.cmd` contained #386's current self-diagnosing body.
2. Temporarily moved `$IX_HOME\cli\ix.cmd` aside and invoked `bin\ix.cmd` through PowerShell/cmd.exe.
3. The launcher exited 1 and printed the intended diagnosis plus:
   `irm https://ix-infra.com/install.ps1 | iex`
4. The output did **not** contain cmd.exe's raw `not recognized as an internal or external command` failure.
5. Restored the target; the launcher again returned `0.9.3`. A deliberately invalid Ix command returned exit 1, also confirming the launcher propagates `%errorlevel%`.

Docker Compose was stubbed so the test did not touch real containers; the release installs, CLI upgrade download/extract/swap, launcher rewrite, and cmd.exe execution were real. Focused regression suite also passes: 45/45 across `windows-launcher.test.ts` and `upgrade-archive-shape.test.ts`.

The original ≤0.8.1 one-way upgrade cannot be changed retroactively, as discussed above, but both the supported forward path and #386 recovery behavior are now confirmed on Windows.

issues.title: [bug] tsconfig paths and baseUrl are ignored during edge resolution
issues.body:
## Description

TypeScript and JavaScript imports configured through `tsconfig.json` or `jsconfig.json` `paths` and `baseUrl` are not used during graph edge resolution. Ix falls back to a repository-wide filename stem, which can select an unrelated file or omit the edge when names are ambiguous.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure `paths` with `"@core": ["src/adapters/worker"]`.
2. Import and call `execute` from `@core`.
3. Add an unrelated `legacy/core.ts` that also exports `execute`.
4. Ingest the repository and inspect `IMPORTS` and `CALLS`.

## Expected behavior

The configured module target resolves to `src/adapters/worker.ts`. A missing configured target remains unresolved instead of falling back to an unrelated stem.

## Actual behavior

Ix can connect both relationships to `legacy/core.ts`, or omit them when multiple stem candidates exist. Equivalent `baseUrl` imports are also not resolved from their configured root.

## CLI output

The wrong target can receive `IMPORTS` and `CALLS` with confidence `0.9`, while the configured target receives no edge.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: main at `fef671c`

issues.title: [bug] renamed TypeScript imports drop inheritance and type-reference edges
issues.body:
## Description

Renamed TypeScript imports can lose inheritance and type-reference relationships even when the imported binding and provider symbol are both known.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Export `User` and `Base` from a provider file.
2. Import them with `import { type User as ExternalUser, Base as LocalBase }`.
3. Use `ExternalUser` in a type annotation and extend `LocalBase`.
4. Ingest the files and inspect `REFERENCES` and `EXTENDS` relationships.

## Expected behavior

The renamed local bindings resolve to the original provider symbols, producing the same relationships as non-renamed imports.

## Actual behavior

The import binding is parsed, but `REFERENCES` and `EXTENDS` relationships are omitted.

## CLI output

The resulting graph contains the file-level `IMPORTS` relationship but no `REFERENCES` or `EXTENDS` relationship for the renamed bindings.

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: main at `fef671c`

issues.title: [bug] ix context crashes on a non-numeric --pick value
issues.body:
## Description

`ix context` does not validate `--pick` as a complete integer before resolving an ambiguous target. A non-numeric value becomes `NaN` and reaches the shared picker, while a partially numeric value such as `1nope` is silently accepted as `1`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Use a graph where the context target resolves to multiple candidates.
2. Run `ix context <target> --pick nope`.
3. Run `ix context <target> --pick 1nope`.

## Expected behavior

Both invalid values are rejected as option errors before target resolution, and the command exits with a non-zero status.

## Actual behavior

`nope` reaches the picker as `NaN` and produces a raw `TypeError` when the selected candidate is read. `1nope` is accepted as candidate `1` because `parseInt` only parses the numeric prefix.

## CLI output

```text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id')
```

## Environment

- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: main at `fef671c`

issues.title: [bug] MCP reports truncated in-process output as success
issues.body:
## Description

The in-process MCP runner reports a command as successful after its output exceeds the configured byte limit. The runner records that the output was truncated, but the final success calculation does not include that state. JSON-backed MCP tools can consequently return an empty structured object as a successful result.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Create an in-process runner with `maxOutputBytes` set to 100.
2. Register a `map` action that prints a JSON payload larger than 100 bytes.
3. Invoke `ix_map` through the MCP server.

## Expected behavior

The runner returns `ok: false`. The MCP result is marked as an error, preserves the truncation reason, and does not include `structuredContent`.

## Actual behavior

The runner returns `ok: true`. The MCP handler discards the warning and returns `{}` as successful `structuredContent`.

## CLI output

```text
[ix mcp] output exceeded 100 bytes and was truncated
```

## Environment
- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Node: v26.7.0
- Ix version: main at fef671c
